We have mass spec m/z 179.0946 (M+?), intensity 100. Likely molecular weight ~179.09. Proton NMR shows signals: two triplets at 2.58 and 2.84 each 2H (likely -CH2-CH2-). A singlet at 3.81 (3H) likely OCH3. Aromatic region: two doublet of doublet of doublet? Actually ddd each 2H at 7.17 and 7.93, total 4 aromatic protons, suggests para-disubstituted benzene (AA'BB') pattern. So aromatic ring with 4 protons, likely para-substituted. The two CH2 triplets suggest an ethyl chain attached to something: maybe -CH2-CH2- attached to carbonyl? The OCH3 suggests a methoxy group attached to aromatic? But aromatic protons are 4, so substituents are para to each other. Could be para-methoxy and para-? Actually methoxy on aromatic gives 3H singlet around 3.8, and aromatic protons would be 4 (AA'BB') if para-methoxy phenyl. Then the ethyl chain could be attached to carbonyl (e.g., ethyl ester). So maybe methyl para-methoxy phenyl? Wait OCH3 is 3.81, typical for methoxy attached to aromatic (anisole). The ethyl chain could be part of an ethyl ester attached to carbonyl attached to aromatic? For example ethyl p-methoxybenzoate (p-anisic acid ethyl ester). That has formula C10H12O3? Actually ethyl p-methoxybenzoate: C10H12O3? Let's compute: p-methoxybenzoic acid is C8H8O3? Wait: p-methoxybenzoic acid: C8H8O3? Actually benzoic acid C7H6O2, add methoxy (OCH3) substituting H gives C8H8O3. Then ethyl ester adds C2H5O, making C10H12O4? Let's compute: p-anisic acid ethyl ester = C9? Let's do: base: benzoic acid C7H6O2. Replace para H with OCH3 adds C1H3O (since H replaced). So C8H9O3? Wait need careful: benzoic acid C7H6O2. Add OCH3 substituent (replace H) gives C8H8O3? Actually OCH3 adds C1H3O, but also adds O? The substituent is -OCH3 attached to ring, adds C1H3O1, but also the H removed from ring, so net C1H3O1. So C8H9O3? Starting C7H6O2 + C1H3O1 = C8H9O3. Then convert acid to ethyl ester: replace OH of COOH with OCH2CH3 (adds C2H5, removes H). So net add C2H4. So final C10H13O3? Wait we also have O from carbonyl already. So final formula C10H12O3? Let's compute: C8H9O3 + C2H4 = C10H13O3. That gives MW: C10=120, H13=13, O3=48 => 181. So 181 not 179. Our mass is 179.09. So maybe formula C10H11NO2? Let's compute: C10H11NO2 = 10*12=120 +11=11 +14=14 +32=32 => 177. Not 179. C10H13NO2 = 120+13+14+32=179. Yes C10H13NO2 matches mass 179. So formula likely C10H13NO2. That matches mass. So we need a molecule with C10H13NO2, containing aromatic ring with 4 protons (para-disubstituted). Substituents: one is methoxy? OCH3 gives O and C and 3H. That accounts for O and C. Another substituent must contain N and maybe carbonyl? The ethyl chain (CH2-CH2) suggests maybe -CH2CH2- attached to carbonyl? Could be -CH2CH2- attached to N? Actually we have two triplets each 2H, typical for -CH2-CH2- attached to heteroatoms (e.g., -CH2-CH2- attached to carbonyl and aromatic). Could be -CH2-CH2- attached to carbonyl (ethyl amide). For example, p-methoxybenzamide with ethyl group? Actually ethyl amide: -C(=O)NHCH2CH3 gives CH3CH2 attached to N, but that would give a quartet and triplet, not two triplets. Two triplets suggests -CH2-CH2- between two heteroatoms (e.g., -O-CH2-CH2-N-). But we have only one O in methoxy, plus carbonyl O. Could be -O-CH2-CH2-NH-? But methoxy is OCH3 not OCH2. So maybe the ethyl chain is part of a N-ethyl group attached to carbonyl: -C(=O)NCH2CH3 gives CH2 (triplet) and CH3 (quartet). Not match.

Two triplets each 2H suggests -CH2-CH2- where each CH2 is adjacent to another CH2 (so both appear as triplets). That is typical for -CH2-CH2- in a chain with no other splitting (e.g., ethylene). Could be -CH2-CH2- attached to aromatic on one side and carbonyl on other side? For example, phenethyl amide? Actually phenethyl group: -CH2-CH2- attached to aromatic gives CH2 next to aromatic (around 2.7) and CH2 next to carbonyl (around 2.5). Both appear as triplets if both are adjacent only to each other. So structure: aromatic-CH2-CH2-CO-N? Wait carbonyl attached to CH2? Ethyl phenylacetate? Phenylacetic acid ethyl ester: Ph-CH2-COOCH2CH3. That has CH2 next to aromatic (singlet? actually appears as a singlet? It is adjacent to carbonyl, not to another CH2). Not two triplets.

Our N present: maybe an amide: -CO-NH-CH2-CH2-? That would give CH2 next to N (triplet) and CH2 next to carbonyl (triplet). Yes. So structure: para-methoxy phenyl attached to carbonyl (amide) with N-ethyl? Wait N-CH2CH2? Actually amide: Ar-CO-NH-CH2-CH2-? But we need N attached to CH2CH2? The N is part of amide, attached to carbonyl and CH2CH2? That would be N-ethyl? Actually N-ethyl amide: Ar-CO-NH-CH2CH3 gives CH2 (quartet) and CH3 (triplet). Not.

If N is attached to CH2CH2 (i.e., N-CH2CH2- something). Could be N-CH2CH2-? But we have only one carbonyl O. So maybe structure: para-methoxy phenyl attached to carbonyl (C=O) which is attached to N-CH2CH2-? That's an amide where the nitrogen is attached to ethylene group (N-CH2CH2-). That would give CH2 next to N (triplet) and CH2 next to something else (maybe another hetero). If the other end of ethylene is attached to something like maybe a terminal amine? But we have only one N.

Thus maybe the molecule is p-anisoyl ethylenediamide? Not.

Let's compute formula for p-anisoyl ethylenediamide? Too many N.

Better: 4-methoxybenzoyl ethylenediamide? Not.

Let's propose structure: 4-methoxybenzamide with N-CH2CH2-? Actually N-CH2CH2-? That would be N-(2-hydroxyethyl)benzamide? That adds O and extra H.

Our formula C10H13NO2: count atoms: C10, H13, N1, O2. Aromatic ring C6H4 (since 4 aromatic H). Add methoxy OCH3 adds C1 H3 O1. So far C7 H7 O1 plus aromatic ring C6 H4? Wait aromatic ring C6 H4 (since 4 H). So total C6+1=7 C, H4+3=7 H, O1. Need carbonyl C=O adds C1 O1. So now C8 H7 O2. Need N1 adds N1. Need remaining C2 H6 to reach C10 H13. Those could be CH2-CH2 (C2 H4) plus maybe extra H? Actually CH2-CH2 gives C2 H4. Then we need H2 more, maybe from NH? The N may have H (NH). So N-H adds H1. Still missing one H. Could be CH3? But we have only CH2-CH2.

Let's sum: aromatic C6 H4, methoxy C1 H3 O1, carbonyl C1 O1, N1 H? (maybe NH), ethylene C2 H4. Total C10, H4+3+4+1=12? plus maybe NH adds H1 =>13. Yes that matches. So structure: para-methoxybenzoyl-NH-CH2-CH2-? Wait carbonyl attached to N (amide) and aromatic (para-methoxy). So it's p-anisoyl amide with ethylene attached to N? Actually N attached to CH2-CH2-? The other end of ethylene maybe H (i.e., N-CH2-CH2-H). That's ethylamine attached to amide: N-CH2-CH3 would be ethyl, not CH2-CH2-H. But CH2-CH2-H is ethyl with terminal H? Actually CH2-CH2-H is ethyl radical, not stable. So maybe N-CH2-CH3 (ethyl) gives CH3 quartet not triplet. So our pattern suggests CH2-CH2 attached to N and carbonyl? Wait N attached to carbonyl, CH2 attached to N, then CH2 attached to something else maybe H? That would be N-CH2-CH3 (ethyl) again.

Thus maybe the ethylene is between aromatic and carbonyl: aromatic-CH2-CH2-CO-N? That would give CH2 next to aromatic (triplet) and CH2 next to carbonyl (triplet). The N is attached to carbonyl only (amide). So structure: p-anisyl-CH2-CH2-CO-NH? But we need N present, O2 present (one carbonyl O, one methoxy O). That fits. So molecule: 4-methoxyphenylacetylamine? Actually phenylacetylamine is Ph-CH2-CO-NH2. That has CH2 next to aromatic (singlet) and carbonyl attached to NH2. Not two CH2.

Our chain is CH2-CH2-CO-NH? Actually aromatic-CH2-CH2-CO-NH? That is phenethyl amide? Wait phenethyl amide would be Ph-CH2-CH2-CO-NH2 (i.e., phenethyl carboxamide). That has aromatic-CH2-CH2-CO-NH2. The CH2 adjacent to aromatic appears as triplet? It is adjacent to CH2 only, so triplet. The CH2 adjacent to carbonyl also adjacent to CH2 only, so triplet. Yes! So that matches two triplets each 2H. So structure: 4-methoxyphenethyl amide (i.e., 4-methoxyphenethyl amide). The amide is -CO-NH2 (no extra substituents). So formula: aromatic C6H4, methoxy C1H3O, ethyl chain C2H4, carbonyl C1O, NH2 adds N1 H2. Total C10 H13 N1 O2. Yes matches. So SMILES: COc1ccc(cc1)CCNC(=O)?? Wait need amide: phenethyl amide is Ph-CH2-CH2-CO-NH2, but our carbonyl is attached to aromatic? Actually phenethyl amide: Ph-CH2-CH2-CO-NH2. So SMILES: O=C(N)CCc1ccc(OC)cc1? Wait order: O=C(N)CCc1ccc(OC)cc1. That is 4-methoxy phenethyl amide. Let's generate: "O=C(N)CCc1ccc(OC)cc1". Validate.
